etymology: From Latin definitio, from definire — to set bounds to, to limit — from de- (completely) + finis (boundary, end). A definition is a fence built around a meaning: it says what a thing is by saying where it stops.
biblical_def: The act of setting the true bounds of a word's meaning — an act Scripture grounds in God himself, who speaks reality into being and then names it: "God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night" (Gen. 1:5). Adam's first recorded work was definitional — naming the creatures under God's authority (Gen. 2:19-20) — which makes right definition part of the dominion mandate, not a neutral academic exercise. Because God's words are "pure words" (Psa. 12:6) and his word is truth (John 17:17), words can carry fixed, knowable meaning; because man is a liar by fallen nature (Rom. 3:4), the corruption of definition is one of sin's oldest tools — the serpent's first move was to blur a definition God had made plain ("Yea, hath God said?"). To define rightly is to submit language to reality as God ordered it; to redefine against him is to "call evil good, and good evil" (Isa. 5:20).
webster_summary: Webster 1828: a brief description of a thing by its properties; in logic, the explication of the essence of a thing; in lexicography, the explanation of the signification of a word.
webster_full: DEFINITION, noun. A brief description of a thing by its properties; as a definition of wit or of a circle.
In logic, the explication of the essence of a thing by its kind and difference.
In lexicography, an explanation of the signification of a word or term, or of what a word is understood to express.

Webster's own 1828 preface treats right definition as a moral and religious duty: he traced English words to their roots because, in his words, language is the instrument by which men receive the knowledge of God's will.
scriptures: Genesis 1:5
And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day.
Genesis 2:19

And out of the ground the LORD God formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air; and brought them unto Adam to see what he would call them: and whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof.
Psalm 12:6
The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
Isaiah 5:20
Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!
John 17:17
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
Matthew 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
corruption_summary: The age does not merely corrupt particular words — it wars against definition itself, treating fixed meaning as oppression and redefinition as liberation.
corruption_paragraphs: The postmodern move is Humpty Dumpty's: "When I use a word, it means just what I choose it to mean." Under that rule the dictionary stops being a fence around reality and becomes a weapon of whoever holds the pen. The last two generations watched the operation run on the load-bearing words — marriage, man, woman, justice, love, hate, violence, safety — each one quietly re-fenced so that the new boundary line includes what God excludes and excludes what God commands.

The tell is that the redefiners rarely argue for the new meaning; they simply institutionalize it — in style guides, search results, HR trainings, and updated dictionary entries — and then treat the old definition as evidence of malice. "That's just your definition" is deployed as if definitions were private property rather than public fences. But a definition that binds no one defines nothing; the phrase is not an argument, it is a refusal to be bound.

Scripture has a name for the endgame: "Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil" (Isa. 5:20). Note that Isaiah's woe is pronounced not on those who do evil but on those who relabel it — the definitional sin is treated as its own category of judgment. This dictionary exists as a counter-measure: every entry is an act of re-fencing, returning words to the boundaries set by the God who named the light before any man had an opinion about it.
roots_summary: Latin definire, to set bounds — the same logic as finis (boundary) in 'finite' and 'final.'
roots_lines: Latin: definitio, from definire — de- (completely) + finis (boundary, end, limit). To define is to declare where a meaning ends.

Greek (concept): horizo (G3724) — to mark a boundary, whence English 'horizon'; used of God's definitional acts: Christ "declared" (horisthentos, marked out by boundary) to be the Son of God, Rom. 1:4.
Hebrew (concept): qara (H7121) — to call, name, proclaim; God's naming of Day, Night, Heaven, Earth, and Seas in Genesis 1 is the original act of definition.
Cognates: finite, final, confine, infinity — all children of finis; a definition is meaning brought inside a fence.
usage: Before we debate whether it is loving, we need the definition of love on the table — God's, not Hallmark's.
He kept shifting the definition mid-argument, so I made him fence the word first and the disagreement collapsed in two sentences.
The catechism's power is in its definitions: a hundred fenced words, and a child armed with them can spot a false gospel before he can drive.

etymology: Academic coinage of the 1970s-80s feminist academy — Nancy Hartsock's "feminist standpoint" (1983), systematized by Sandra Harding — adapting the Marxist claim that the proletariat sees class reality more truly than its masters. Standpoint (where one stands) + epistemology (theory of knowledge): the theory that knowledge is determined by social position.
biblical_def: The claim that truth is indexed to social location — that the marginalized possess privileged access to knowledge by virtue of their oppression, so that "lived experience" outranks argument, evidence, and testimony from outside the favored group. Scripture flatly contradicts both halves. First, truth is grounded in God, not in position: his word is truth (John 17:17), and it addresses kings and beggars on identical terms. Second, Scripture forbids epistemic partiality in BOTH directions: "thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour" (Lev. 19:15) — a verse that anticipates and condemns the standpoint move by name, since tilting the scales toward the poor man's testimony is the form of partiality the modern academy baptizes. Experience is real data, but it arrives through a heart that is "deceitful above all things" (Jer. 17:9) and must be weighed: "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him" (Prov. 18:17). Every claim — from any standpoint — faces the same court: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1 Thes. 5:21).
webster_summary: No Webster 1828 entry — the phrase is a late-20th-century academic coinage. Webster would have filed the underlying questions under KNOWLEDGE and TESTIMONY, both of which his definitions ground in evidence rather than in the witness's social station.
webster_full: STANDPOINT EPISTEMOLOGY, noun phrase. Feminist-Marxist theory of knowledge: Hartsock's 'The Feminist Standpoint' (1983), Harding's 'strong objectivity' (1991) — knowledge is socially situated; marginalized positions yield epistemic privilege.
The pipeline runs Marx (class consciousness) → feminist standpoint theory → critical race theory's 'unique voice of color' → the popular idiom 'listen to lived experience.'

In practice it functions as an unanswerable-argument machine: disagreement from outside the favored standpoint is reclassified as evidence of the speaker's blindness, so the thesis can never be falsified — the mark of ideology rather than knowledge.
scriptures: Leviticus 19:15
Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour.
Proverbs 18:17
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
Jeremiah 17:9
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
2 Corinthians 13:1
This is the third time I am coming to you. In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established.
1 Thessalonians 5:21
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
John 7:24
Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.
corruption_summary: Not itself a corrupted word but a corrupting framework — it relocates the ground of truth from God's revelation to group identity, and it has leaked from the seminar room into the church.
corruption_paragraphs: The framework entered evangelical spaces wearing pastoral clothes: "we need to listen to marginalized voices" — which, as a call to hear testimony and examine it, is simply Proverbs 18:17. But standpoint epistemology smuggles in a second clause: that the testimony may not be searched, because searching it is itself oppression. At that point listening has been converted from the beginning of judgment into the end of it, and Lev. 19:15's forbidden partiality has been rebranded as righteousness.

The practical fruit in the church: staff trainings where disagreement is recoded as 'fragility,' testimonies that function as trump cards, and shepherds afraid to weigh an accusation because the accuser holds the favored standpoint. Scripture's witness-law is the antidote — two or three witnesses (2 Cor. 13:1), cross-examination (Prov. 18:17), no respect of persons in either direction (Lev. 19:15) — a jurisprudence that protects the genuinely oppressed far better than epistemic privilege does, because it cannot be captured by whoever shouts their standing loudest.

The deepest error is theological: standpoint epistemology is a doctrine of revelation with the Revealer deleted. It correctly senses that fallen man's knowing is corrupted and partial — total depravity reaches the mind — but instead of looking up to the God whose word cuts through every situated heart, it crowns one class of situated hearts as the oracle. The Reformed answer is not that the comfortable see clearly, but that NO flesh sees clearly, "but God" (Eph. 2:4) speaks — and his word judges every standpoint, including the marginal one.
roots_summary: Marxist class-consciousness, retooled by the feminist academy (Hartsock 1983, Harding 1991), flowing into CRT's 'voice of color' and the street idiom 'lived experience.'
roots_lines: Marx/Lukács: the proletariat's position grants truer sight of class reality — the template for all standpoint claims.
Hartsock 1983: 'The Feminist Standpoint' — women's social position yields epistemic privilege about gendered reality.
Harding 1991: 'strong objectivity' — research should START from marginalized lives; neutrality is recast as bias.
CRT adoption: the 'unique voice of color' thesis — see [[critical-race-theory]] — and from there the popular commandment to 'center lived experience.'

Biblical counter-grammar: mishpat (H4941, judgment) bound to witnesses and evidence; prosopolepsia (G4382, respect of persons) condemned in James 2:1-9 — partiality is sin regardless of which face is favored.
usage: The moment a claim cannot be questioned without the questioner being indicted, you are no longer dealing with testimony — that is standpoint epistemology doing its work.
Lev. 19:15 forbids tilting the scale toward the mighty AND toward the poor; standpoint epistemology calls the second tilt justice, and Moses calls it unrighteousness.
She said her lived experience settled the matter; the elder gently answered that experience is a witness to be heard and weighed, not a verdict to be obeyed.

etymology: From Latin victima — a beast appointed for sacrifice, the animal brought to the altar. The word entered English through sacrificial religion and only later widened to mean any person destroyed or injured by another's act. The oldest meaning still governs the deepest one: at the center of the faith stands a true Victim, the Lamb appointed before the foundation of the world.
biblical_def: One who actually suffers wrong at the hands of another — the man stripped and left half dead on the Jericho road (Luke 10:30), Abel whose blood cried from the ground (Gen. 4:10), Naboth under false witnesses, Uriah under a king's pen. Scripture never blinks at the reality of victims: God names himself "the helper of the fatherless" (Psa. 10:14), hears the cry of the afflicted widow (Ex. 22:22-23), and prices the blood of the poor as "precious... in his sight" (Psa. 72:14). Biblical justice exists in large part FOR victims — open thy mouth for the dumb (Prov. 31:8) — and the avenger-of-blood and cities of refuge were a whole legal architecture built around innocent blood. But Scripture does two further things the age refuses to do together: it insists victimhood is a wrong suffered, not a righteousness possessed — the victim needs Christ's blood exactly as his oppressor does — and it refuses to let victimhood be destiny: Joseph, the Bible's archetypal victim, ends the story saying "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good" (Gen. 50:20). The supreme Victim is Christ himself — oppressed, afflicted, opening not his mouth (Isa. 53:7), reviled yet not reviling (1 Pet. 2:23) — who did not weaponize his wounds but redeemed through them, and rose.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: a living being sacrificed to some deity or in a religious rite; something destroyed or sacrificed in the pursuit of an object; a person destroyed or grievously injured by another.
webster_full: VICTIM, noun. A living being sacrificed to some deity, or in the performance of a religious rite; usually, some beast slain in sacrifice; but human beings have been slain by some nations, for the purpose of appeasing the wrath or conciliating the favor of some deity.
Something destroyed; something sacrificed in the pursuit of an object.
A person or thing destroyed or sacrificed by, or suffering grievous injury from, another; as a victim of fraud, of oppression, of war.
Note the order: Webster's first sense is sacrificial. The word's center of gravity is the altar, not the grievance.
scriptures: Genesis 4:10
And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground.
Exodus 22:22-23
Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child. If thou afflict them in any wise, and they cry at all unto me, I will surely hear their cry;
Psalm 10:14
Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand: the poor committeth himself unto thee; thou art the helper of the fatherless.
Proverbs 31:8-9
Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction. Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.
Isaiah 53:7
He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.
Genesis 50:20
But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
1 Peter 2:23
Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:
corruption_summary: The age corrupts the word from both ends — inflating victimhood into an identity and a currency, or cynically denying that real victims exist at all. Scripture rebukes both.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is inflation. Where the word once named a wrong suffered, it now names a status held — renewable, rankable, and spendable. Grievance becomes capital; the standpoint theorists supply the epistemology (the victim sees truest — see [[standpoint-epistemology]]), the bureaucracies supply the incentives, and soon the title is claimed most loudly by those wronged least, while the actually crushed — the trafficked, the aborted, the persecuted church — are crowded out of their own category. When victimhood pays, counterfeits multiply; and every counterfeit cheapens the coin the real victim must spend to be heard.

The second corruption is the backlash that overcorrects: the sneer that 'there are no victims, only volunteers,' the reflex that every sufferer must have earned it. That is the theology of Job's friends, and God's verdict on it was wrath (Job 42:7). Scripture will not allow it: blood cries from the ground and God hears (Gen. 4:10); the widow's cry triggers his own avenging (Ex. 22:23-24). A man hardened against real victims is not based; he is unlike his God, who took up the victim's cause so personally that he became one.

The biblical balance is severe in both directions. To the wronged: your suffering is seen, priced, and will be requited — and it is a wound, not a crown; only one Victim's blood justifies, and it is not yours. To the comfortable: the test of pure religion remains the fatherless and the widow (James 1:27), and the mouth God commands you to open is for the dumb, not for yourself. The gospel's final word to victims is Joseph's and Christ's: wrong is real, God means it for good, and resurrection — not retribution and not curated grievance — is the end of the story.
roots_summary: Latin victima, the sacrificial beast — the word begins at the altar, climaxes at the Cross, and only degenerates into a status symbol when severed from both.
roots_lines: Latin: victima — the beast appointed for sacrifice; cognate with the religious vocabulary of consecration, not of complaint.
Hebrew (concept): anaw / ani (H6041) — the afflicted, poor, oppressed whom God defends; dam naqi, innocent blood, which the LORD will not hold guiltless.
Greek (concept): amnos (G286), the Lamb — "behold the Lamb of God" (John 1:29); the New Testament's victim-word is a sacrifice-word, fulfilled at the Cross.

KJV note: the English word 'victim' never appears in the KJV — Scripture speaks instead of the afflicted, the oppressed, the fatherless, and the Lamb, keeping persons and sacrifice distinct until they meet in Christ.
usage: The church must be the safest place on earth for a real victim and the hardest place on earth to profit from a fake claim — Prov. 31:8 and Prov. 18:17 in the same building.
He suffered a genuine wrong, and the men around him made sure of two things: that justice was pursued, and that the wound never became his name.
Christ is the only Victim whose wounds justify anyone — which frees the wronged man to seek justice without needing his suffering to be his righteousness.
